clinicalPearls: Consider in an older adult or a postpartum woman with new-onset spontaneous bleeding and no personal or family history of a bleeding disorder.
Bleeding is typically extensive subcutaneous, muscle and soft-tissue haematoma with mucosal bleeding, in contrast to the haemarthroses that dominate congenital haemophilia.
The screening abnormality is an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time, thrombin time, fibrinogen and platelet count.
The prolonged aPTT fails to correct on a mixing study, and the inhibitor is characteristically time- and temperature-dependent, so correction worsens after incubation.
Factor VIII activity is reduced and the inhibitor is quantified using the Bethesda (or Nijmegen-modified Bethesda) assay.
The cause is a polyclonal IgG autoantibody against factor VIII; roughly half of cases are idiopathic and the remainder are linked to malignancy, the postpartum period, autoimmune disease or drugs.

Acute bleeding is controlled with bypassing agents (recombinant activated factor VII or activated prothrombin complex concentrate) or recombinant porcine factor VIII rather than standard human factor VIII.

Durable control requires eradication of the inhibitor with immunosuppression such as corticosteroids alone or combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab, alongside treatment of any underlying trigger.
reference.pathophysiology: Acquired haemophilia A arises from the spontaneous development of polyclonal IgG autoantibodies, most often of the IgG1 and IgG4 subclasses, directed against coagulation factor VIII, particularly its A2 and C2 domains that mediate binding to factor IXa and to phospholipid. Unlike the alloantibodies seen in congenital haemophilia, these autoantibodies typically show complex, non-linear (type 2) inhibitory kinetics, so measurable residual factor VIII activity often coexists with severe clinical bleeding and the inhibitor never fully neutralises the factor in a simple proportional manner. Loss of functional factor VIII cripples the intrinsic tenase complex and the amplification phase of thrombin generation, producing a marked bleeding tendency. The breakdown of immune tolerance is frequently associated with a triggering state such as underlying malignancy, the peripartum period, autoimmune disorders or certain drugs, although a large proportion of cases, especially in the elderly, remain idiopathic.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital haemophilia A complicated by an alloantibody inhibitor
Lupus anticoagulant or antiphospholipid syndrome, which prolongs the aPTT but predisposes to thrombosis rather than bleeding
Von Willebrand disease, including acquired von Willebrand syndrome
Other acquired factor inhibitors, for example against factor V or factor XI
Heparin contamination or the effect of a direct oral anticoagulant
Liver disease or vitamin K deficiency, which also prolong the prothrombin time
additionalInvestigations: Mixing study with both immediate and incubated (delayed) sampling to demonstrate a time-dependent inhibitor
Factor VIII activity assay together with assays of the other intrinsic-pathway factors to localise the defect
Bethesda or Nijmegen-modified Bethesda assay to quantify the inhibitor titre
Testing to exclude a lupus anticoagulant, such as a dilute Russell viper venom time
Von Willebrand factor antigen and activity to exclude acquired von Willebrand syndrome
Age-appropriate malignancy screening and autoimmune serology to seek an underlying association
Baseline full blood count with renal and liver function before starting immunosuppression
redFlags: Rapidly expanding muscle or retroperitoneal haematoma causing compartment syndrome or haemodynamic compromise
Airway compromise from neck, tongue or retropharyngeal bleeding
Severe mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding with a falling haemoglobin
reference.prognosis: Mortality is significant, driven early by haemorrhage and later by infection related to immunosuppression, yet with prompt inhibitor eradication most patients achieve durable remission. Relapse can occur, so continued haematological follow-up is required.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the isolated prolonged aPTT as a lupus anticoagulant and either withholding treatment or, worse, starting anticoagulation.
Omitting an incubated mixing study, so that a time-dependent factor VIII inhibitor is missed.
Attempting to overcome a high-titre inhibitor with standard human factor VIII concentrate or desmopressin, which is usually ineffective.
Performing intramuscular injections, arterial punctures or invasive procedures that precipitate catastrophic bleeding.
Dismissing new bruising in an elderly patient as senile purpura or an anticoagulant effect and delaying coagulation testing.
references: International consensus recommendations on acquired haemophilia
National haemophilia and bleeding disorder management guidelines
management: Control acute bleeding with bypassing agents such as recombinant activated factor VII or activated prothrombin complex concentrate, or with recombinant porcine factor VIII
Eradicate the factor VIII autoantibody with immunosuppression using corticosteroids, often combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab
Avoid intramuscular injections, arterial punctures and non-essential invasive procedures that provoke bleeding
Investigate and treat any underlying trigger such as malignancy, autoimmune disease or a causative drug
Monitor factor VIII activity and Bethesda inhibitor titre to gauge response, with anti-infective prophylaxis during immunosuppression
Haematology-led follow-up after remission to detect relapse
